name: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
presentation: A patient describes burning pain and tingling in the sole of the foot and the toes, worse after prolonged standing or walking and sometimes at night, with relief on resting or removing shoes. Sensation may be reduced on the sole while the dorsum of the foot and the heel are normal, and in long-standing cases the small muscles of the foot are wasted and the toes clawed. Tapping behind the medial malleolus reproduces the tingling.

deficits.distribution: sole of the foot and toes (medial and lateral plantar nerves)
deficits.sign: Burning paresthesias and sensory loss of the sole, sparing the dorsum; heel sometimes spared
Pain worse with standing and walking, Tinel sign at the flexor retinaculum
Weakness and wasting of the abductor hallucis and toe flexors with clawing in chronic cases; calf muscles and ankle reflex normal

reasoning: Behind the medial malleolus the tibial nerve passes beneath the flexor retinaculum in the tarsal tunnel, with the tendons of the tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus and the posterior tibial vessels, and there divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves for the sole and the intrinsic muscles and the calcaneal branch for the heel. Compression within the tunnel by tenosynovitis, a ganglion, varicosities, a bony spur after an ankle fracture, hindfoot valgus or a tight retinaculum produces the plantar sensory symptoms and, later, intrinsic muscle weakness. The muscles of the calf and the ankle reflex are supplied by the tibial nerve above the tunnel and are unaffected, which separates the syndrome from a proximal tibial or sciatic lesion, and the dorsum of the foot is supplied by the peroneal nerves and is spared, which separates it from a polyneuropathy that would involve the whole foot symmetrically on both sides. The calcaneal branch often leaves the nerve above the retinaculum, so heel sensation may be preserved. An S1 radiculopathy affects the sole too but adds calf weakness, an absent ankle reflex and back pain. The deficit is peripheral and ipsilateral. Electrodiagnosis is technically demanding, and the diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern, a positive Tinel sign, imaging of the tunnel and the response to a local anesthetic block.

imagingFindings.finding: Prolonged distal latencies of the medial and lateral plantar nerves with denervation of the abductor hallucis and abductor digiti minimi; normal peroneal and proximal tibial conduction.
Ganglion, varicosities, tenosynovitis, lipoma or accessory muscle within the tarsal tunnel compressing the nerve on axial T2.
Talocalcaneal coalition, exostosis or malunited fracture narrowing the tunnel.

mimics.name: Plantar fasciitis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pain under the heel worst on first steps, no sensory loss or Tinel sign

mimics.name: Distal polyneuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral, symmetric, dorsum involved, reduced ankle reflexes

mimics.name: S1 radiculopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Back pain, calf weakness, absent ankle jerk

mimics.name: Morton neuroma
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pain between the metatarsal heads, focal

management: Orthotics to correct hindfoot valgus, activity modification, anti-inflammatory measures
Steroid injection into the tunnel for inflammatory causes
Surgical release for a demonstrable mass or persistent symptoms with electrodiagnostic confirmation

imagingHint.label: tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus (virtual)
